messages.subject: Custom Sampler Without Calculate Function
parts:
Hello, 

I am coding a custom sampler that does not use the calculate function, it only updates the target node values. In this case do I need to run,

calculate(model, model$getDependencies(target))

At the very end of the function?

Thanks!

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Custom Sampler Without Calculate Function
parts:
Hi Dirk,

The rules for a sampler are that it can expect upon entry to have the model in a fully calculated state (so, for example, model$getLogProb(nodes) can be used reliably, since this pulls cached values of log probs without calculating them) and to have the mvSaved and the model be fully in sync (all values matching).  That means that for a sampler to work correctly in the system (assuming it might be used amid other samplers in the MCMC configuration), it must ensure those two conditions are met again before it exits, for the benefit of the next sampler.

Specifically, if you have a sampler that changes the value of model[[target]], it is the sampler's responsibility to ensure those conditions upon exit.  The typical way to do so is
In setup code: 
calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
In run code:
model$calculate( calcNodes ) ## preferred syntax.  Usually model$getDependencies(target) is created in the setup function.
nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, rowTo = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)

Of course, it would be possible to set up multiple samplers that violate the system's rules if they work in concert and you are clear what you are doing, but otherwise it is highly recommended to follow the system.

Let us know further questions.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Custom Sampler Without Calculate Function
parts:
Hi Dirk,

Yes, we've run into this kind of need as well.  I can suggest two ways to do this.

First, you can make a single vector of all dependencies and then vectors of which indices are needed in which case.

Then your run code would have something like
for(j in 1:numDeps[i]) {
   logProb <- logProb + model$calculate(calcNodes[ depIndices[i, j])
}

In this case, you would be iterating over each dependency yourself

Second, and more generally, you can make a nimbleFunctionList of nimbleFunction objects (you would need a nimbleFunction for this purpose with a nimbleFunctionVirtual to serve as a base class) that manage each set of dependencies you need.  You can look up nimbleFunctionList in the User Manual and see examples in nimble's source code.

The your run code would have something like

myCalculators[[i]]$run()

for the i-th set of dependencies you need.

-Perry

logProb <- 0

}

Of course if you don't need the logProb sum you can omit it.

Perry

That's helpful.  So here's what is going on.

The NIMBLE compiler, what we call the C++ code-generation system, does its best to look at types of objects created in setup code and used in run code or other methods.  It needed to decide what static C++ type to create for each R object.

In the case of matrix, the default element type of R's matrix() is logical:

storage.mode(matrix(nrow = 2, ncol = 2)) ## "logical"

What is really needed is to create a matrix in R with double (or integer, if you want) elements in your setup code.  When you assign some elements to c(0.9, 0.9), that happens dynamically in R, so by the time NIMBLE inspects it, it has storage.mode "double".

Another option would be

matrix(numeric(), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)

which we can see has double-precision elements.

storage.mode(matrix(numeric(), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)) # "double"

When your run code has a vectorized operation, nimble generates C++ that uses the Eigen library, and to do so it attempts to generate C++ that converts between types explicitly, which is needed in writing Eigen code.  That is when the error messages about loss of type information are generated.  I want to take a closer look because the way it errored out on you was not very friendly.

When your run code has only scalar assignments, nimble generates C++ that relies on automatic type-casting in C/C++. That is, scalar assignment from a logical to a double, for example, will compile but will not give you what you want, which is what you observed.

So the practical point of the story is to ensure that objects created in setup code that you need to use as double-precision are in fact double precision in R.

You can create a matrix in run code with nimMatrix (which "matrix" will automatically be converted to), which provides some more fine-grained control, so be sure to read help(nimMatrix).  But if you create it in setup code, it will persist across run calls, like member data of an object.

HTH.
-Perry

On Thursday, May 28, 2020 at 1:58:16 PM UTC-4, pdevalpine wrote:
Hi Dirk,

The rules for a sampler are that it can expect upon entry to have the model in a fully calculated state (so, for example, model$getLogProb(nodes) can be used reliably, since this pulls cached values of log probs without calculating them) and to have the mvSaved and the model be fully in sync (all values matching).  That means that for a sampler to work correctly in the system (assuming it might be used amid other samplers in the MCMC configuration), it must ensure those two conditions are met again before it exits, for the benefit of the next sampler.

Specifically, if you have a sampler that changes the value of model[[target]], it is the sampler's responsibility to ensure those conditions upon exit.  The typical way to do so is
In setup code: 
calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
In run code:
model$calculate( calcNodes ) ## preferred syntax.  Usually model$getDependencies(target) is created in the setup function.
nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, rowTo = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)

Of course, it would be possible to set up multiple samplers that violate the system's rules if they work in concert and you are clear what you are doing, but otherwise it is highly recommended to follow the system.

Let us know further questions.

-Perry
